title: My ResearchEd Toronto Presentation
author: Sean Morrisey
summary: Sean Morrisey, a Grade 5 teacher, recounts presenting a workshop on spelling instruction at ResearchEd Toronto with Anita Archer sitting front and centre. He uses the occasion to describe a four-minute vocabulary and spelling routine built on the work of Archer, Margaret McKeown and Elfrieda Hiebert. The routine teaches a pair of contrasting words, here optional and mandatory, with choral responses, student-friendly definitions and a final spelling choice on mini-whiteboards. He grounds it in Charles Perfetti's Lexical Quality Hypothesis, which holds that skilled reading depends on precise, well-connected word representations. A further layer has students write related words, which prompts retrieval and semantic mapping. He closes by urging teachers to build on research but still take some risks in the classroom.
points: The routine pairs semantically contrasting words so students learn a shared concept rather than two isolated definitions.
Choral response and concise student-friendly definitions are used to secure full participation and begin word mapping.
Spelling is folded into vocabulary teaching, justified by Perfetti's Lexical Quality Hypothesis about linking spelling, pronunciation and meaning.
Asking students to write related words on mini-whiteboards adds retrieval practice and semantic categorising at little cost in time.
Morrisey credits a former student for the related-words idea, showing how classroom practice can extend research-based routines.
quotes: ResearchEd is an international organization that aims to close the gap between educational research and what actually happens in the classroom.

Learning words requires robust vocabulary instruction which includes meaningful explanations, multiple exposures, opportunities to practice with words, and using sophisticated language in your daily teacher talk.
Anita Archer talks about introducing a word and having students chorally say the word back. This encourages 100% participation and active engagement.
Presenting words in contrast pairs gets kids to think about categories highlighting Elfreida Hiebert’s work in vocabulary instruction.

I am a strong proponent of Charles Perfetti’s Lexical Quality Hypothesis. It proposes that skilled reading depends on having precise, well-connected representations of words in memory, including their spelling, pronunciation, and meaning, allowing for quick and accurate word recognition and comprehension.
Having student say the word is crucial. This begins the word mapping process.

I encourage students to write words that are related to the correct answer. This further supports active engagement, has students retrieve past words that they have learned (spelling included), and think at a higher level by linking words into a category (semantic mapping).
Yes, research should provide the foundation, but try some things out in the classroom that haven’t been tried before. You might find it works especially well.
